title: Screening for Type 2 Diabetes in Adults
source: Sample corpus — summary in the style of ADA Standards of Care
text: Adults aged 35 to 70 years who have overweight or obesity should be screened for type 2 diabetes, and screening should be considered earlier in people with a first-degree relative with diabetes, a history of gestational diabetes, or high-risk ethnicity. Screening can be performed with HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, or a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test, and no single test is preferred in all settings. An HbA1c of 6.5% or higher, a fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, or a 2-hour glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher supports a diagnosis when confirmed on repeat testing in the absence of unequivocal symptoms. People with prediabetes, defined by an HbA1c between 5.7% and 6.4%, should be retested at least annually and offered structured lifestyle support. If results are normal, repeat screening every 3 years is reasonable, with more frequent testing when risk factors change.

title: Intensive Lifestyle Intervention for Prediabetes
source: Sample corpus — summary in the style of a diabetes prevention trial report
text: Structured lifestyle programmes that achieve 5% to 7% body weight loss and at least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity per week reduce progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes substantially over 3 years. The intervention emphasises dietary change, regular activity, behavioural self-monitoring, and frequent contact in the first 6 months. Benefits were observed across age groups, although adherence declined over time and weight regain was common without maintenance sessions. Metformin may be considered for people at particularly high risk, especially those with a body mass index above 35 or a prior history of gestational diabetes. Programmes delivered in community settings achieved smaller but still meaningful weight loss compared with the original trial setting.

title: Diagnosis and Thresholds for Hypertension
source: Sample corpus — summary in the style of ACC/AHA hypertension guidance
text: Hypertension is diagnosed when blood pressure is persistently elevated on repeated measurement, using an average of two or more readings taken on two or more occasions. Normal blood pressure is below 120/80 mmHg, elevated blood pressure is 120 to 129 systolic with diastolic below 80 mmHg, stage 1 hypertension is 130 to 139 systolic or 80 to 89 diastolic, and stage 2 hypertension is 140/90 mmHg or higher. Out-of-office measurement with ambulatory or home monitoring is recommended to confirm the diagnosis and to exclude white-coat hypertension before starting lifelong treatment. Accurate technique matters: the patient should sit quietly for 5 minutes, use a correctly sized cuff, and avoid caffeine and smoking beforehand. Treatment thresholds and targets are then set according to overall cardiovascular risk, diabetes, and kidney disease.

title: Home Blood Pressure Monitoring in Practice
source: Sample corpus — primary care implementation summary
text: Home blood pressure monitoring, performed twice daily for 7 days with the first day discarded, predicts cardiovascular events better than a single clinic reading and helps identify masked hypertension. Patients need a validated upper-arm device, a correctly sized cuff, and written instructions to record readings without selectively omitting high values. Average home readings of 135/85 mmHg or higher are generally considered hypertensive. Sharing readings electronically with the practice improved medication titration in several implementation studies, but only when a clinician reviewed the data on a defined schedule. Home monitoring does not replace ambulatory monitoring where nocturnal blood pressure or diagnostic uncertainty is the main concern.

title: Early Recognition and First-Hour Management of Sepsis
source: Sample corpus — summary in the style of Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidance
text: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, and early recognition is the strongest determinant of outcome that clinicians can influence. Screening tools such as NEWS2, qSOFA, and SIRS criteria identify patients who need urgent assessment, although none is sufficiently sensitive to be used alone. Blood cultures and serum lactate should be obtained promptly, ideally before antibiotics, provided this does not delay treatment. Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be given within 1 hour for patients with septic shock or a high likelihood of sepsis. Initial fluid resuscitation with balanced crystalloids, commonly 30 mL/kg in the first 3 hours for hypotension, should be guided by repeated assessment rather than given blindly, and vasopressors are started if mean arterial pressure remains below 65 mmHg.

title: Early Warning Scores on General Wards
source: Sample corpus — hospital systems evaluation summary
text: Aggregate early warning scores such as NEWS2 combine respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, systolic blood pressure, pulse, and consciousness into a single score that triggers escalating observation and review. Implementation reduced unexpected cardiac arrests in several before-and-after studies, but effects on mortality were inconsistent. Alert fatigue is a recognised problem: a high proportion of alerts occur in patients already known to be deteriorating, and response quality depends more on staffing and escalation culture than on the score itself. Scores perform less well in patients with chronic hypoxaemia, where individualised oxygen targets are needed. Early warning scores support, and do not replace, clinical concern — a worried nurse or relative should trigger review regardless of the score.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Radiology: Benefits and Limitations
source: Sample corpus — imaging informatics review summary
text: Deep learning systems for radiology imaging have matched or exceeded average human performance on narrow tasks such as detecting lung nodules on CT, identifying diabetic retinopathy on fundus images, and flagging intracranial haemorrhage for priority reporting. The clearest practical benefit is workflow: triage models that move urgent studies to the top of a worklist reduce reporting delay for time-critical findings. Performance commonly drops when a model trained at one hospital is tested at another, because scanners, protocols, and patient populations differ — external validation is therefore essential before deployment. Models can also learn shortcuts, such as image markers or portable-scanner artefacts, rather than the pathology itself. Regulatory approval for a detection task does not establish that patient outcomes improve, and prospective outcome studies remain relatively few compared with retrospective accuracy studies.

title: Evaluating Diagnostic AI Before Clinical Deployment
source: Sample corpus — clinical AI evaluation framework summary
text: A diagnostic AI system should be evaluated in stages: technical validation on held-out data, external validation at independent sites, silent prospective evaluation where predictions are recorded but not acted on, and finally an impact study measuring patient or workflow outcomes. Reporting should include sensitivity, specificity, calibration, and performance in subgroups defined by age, sex, ethnicity, and comorbidity, because average accuracy can hide clinically important disparities. Data leakage between training and test sets, and labels derived from billing codes rather than confirmed diagnosis, are common sources of inflated results. Post-deployment monitoring is required because performance drifts as equipment, protocols, and populations change. Clinicians remain accountable for decisions made with AI support, so the system should present its output in a way that makes disagreement and override easy.

title: Colorectal Cancer Screening: Age and Modalities
source: Sample corpus — summary in the style of USPSTF screening guidance
text: Adults at average risk should be screened for colorectal cancer from age 45 to 75 years, with screening selectively offered between 76 and 85 years based on prior screening history and overall health. Accepted strategies include colonoscopy every 10 years, annual faecal immunochemical testing, and stool DNA testing at longer intervals, among others. A positive stool-based test is not a diagnosis and must be followed by colonoscopy to complete the screening process. People with a first-degree relative diagnosed before age 60, a hereditary syndrome such as Lynch syndrome, or long-standing inflammatory bowel disease need earlier and more intensive surveillance. Screening reduces both incidence, by removing precancerous polyps, and mortality, but benefits are realised only when follow-up and treatment pathways are completed.

title: Lung Cancer Screening with Low-Dose CT
text: Annual low-dose CT screening reduces lung cancer mortality in adults at high risk because of smoking history, and eligibility is generally defined by age between 50 and 80 years, at least a 20 pack-year history, and currently smoking or quitting within the past 15 years. Screening should be combined with smoking cessation support at every contact, since quitting remains the most effective way to reduce risk. False positives are common and most positive scans do not represent cancer, so structured nodule protocols are used to limit unnecessary invasive procedures. Overdiagnosis and radiation exposure are real harms that should be discussed before enrolment. Screening is not recommended when a person has a health problem that substantially limits life expectancy or the ability to have curative lung surgery.

title: Screening for Depression in Primary Care
source: Sample corpus — summary in the style of USPSTF / NICE primary care guidance
text: Screening for depression in adults in primary care, including pregnant and postpartum people and older adults, is recommended when systems are in place for accurate diagnosis, effective treatment, and follow-up. The PHQ-2 is commonly used as a first step, followed by the PHQ-9, where a score of 10 or higher has reasonable sensitivity and specificity for major depression. A screening score alone is not a diagnosis: a clinical interview must establish duration, functional impairment, and exclude bipolar disorder and medical causes such as hypothyroidism. Screening without treatment pathways shows little benefit, which is why guidance ties the recommendation to adequate support systems. Suicide risk should be assessed directly whenever depression is identified, and safety planning and urgent pathways should follow local protocol.

title: Statins for Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease
source: Sample corpus — summary in the style of USPSTF prevention guidance
text: Statin therapy for primary prevention is recommended for adults aged 40 to 75 years who have one or more cardiovascular risk factors and an estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk of 10% or higher, and may be offered selectively when estimated risk is between 7.5% and 10%. Absolute benefit grows with baseline risk, so two people taking the same statin can expect very different gains. Common adverse effects include muscle symptoms, although blinded trials suggest many reported symptoms occur equally with placebo, and serious liver injury is rare. A small increase in incident diabetes has been observed, mainly in people already close to the diagnostic threshold. Decisions should be shared, taking account of patient preference, competing risks, and the option of additional risk markers such as coronary artery calcium where guidelines support it.

title: Screening and Monitoring in Chronic Kidney Disease
source: Sample corpus — nephrology summary in the style of KDIGO guidance
text: Chronic kidney disease is defined by abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for more than 3 months, and is classified using estimated glomerular filtration rate and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio together. Screening is targeted at people at increased risk, including those with diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or a family history of kidney failure, rather than the general population. Both eGFR and albuminuria independently predict progression and cardiovascular events, so measuring only creatinine misses early disease in many patients. Blood pressure control, renin-angiotensin system inhibition in albuminuric disease, and SGLT2 inhibitors in appropriate patients slow progression. Monitoring frequency increases as eGFR falls, and referral is indicated for rapidly declining function, heavy proteinuria, or diagnostic uncertainty.

title: Recognising Stroke and the Importance of Time
source: Sample corpus — acute stroke pathway summary
text: Public recognition campaigns use the FAST test — face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty, time to call emergency services — because treatment benefit in acute ischaemic stroke falls rapidly with delay. Intravenous thrombolysis is generally given within 4.5 hours of symptom onset in eligible patients, and mechanical thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion can benefit selected patients up to 24 hours after onset. A non-contrast CT scan is performed immediately on arrival to exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis. Not every FAST-positive presentation is a stroke: hypoglycaemia, migraine, and seizures are common mimics and are part of the initial assessment. Patients with transient symptoms that resolve still need urgent same-day assessment, because short-term risk of a completed stroke is highest in the first days.
